data.title: Trump appointee Bill Pulte’s housing agency obstructed watchdog, report says
data.description:
By Marisa Taylor and Chris Prentice

A top US housing regulator led by Trump appointee Bill Pulte refused to provide records to its internal watchdog, obstructing congressionally mandated reviews of its oversight of Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and other housing lenders, according to a report reviewed by Reuters on Friday.

The assertions escalate the Federal Housing Finance Agency's confrontation with the watchdog, and come amid broader efforts by President Donald Trump’s administration to weaken government inspectors general whose mission is to root out waste, fraud, and mismanagement across federal agencies and departments.

The report, prepared by the FHFA's Office of Inspector General (OIG) earlier this month, alleges that the agency interfered with its independence and blocked its oversight of mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

The report called the obstruction "unprecedented."

It said the FHFA had refused to provide records and information in response to the watchdog’s requests during at least three separate evaluations, including the agency’s oversight of a lender involved in multifamily loans that had defaulted in June 2024.

The report was sent to lawmakers on Friday.

A spokesperson for the FHFA called the OIG’s allegations incorrect, saying it has "readily produced" information and cooperated with its watchdog.

For instance, the agency spokesperson said, its staff had completed 56 document requests and attended 16 separate hour-long meetings for just three recent reviews.

"FHFA is proud of its record of respecting the independence and role of the OIG and continues to do so," the spokesperson said.

The FHFA oversees the Federal Home Loan Banks as well as Fannie and Freddie, government-sponsored enterprises that have been under FHFA’s direct oversight since the 2008 financial crisis. The enterprises underpin the US housing market by backing the majority of all mortgages.

Under Pulte, however, the historically low-profile agency has become increasingly politicized. The agency has helped lead efforts to target perceived enemies of the president, including with criminal referrals of alleged mortgage fraud by Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and New York Attorney General Letitia James. They have both denied wrongdoing. Pulte has defended the allegations as efforts to root out fraud in mortgage markets.

Pulte, a scion of a homebuilding empire, was a surprise pick to lead the housing regulator, but has become a trusted confidant of Trump’s.

Shortly after being confirmed as FHFA director in March 2025, Pulte took the unprecedented step of appointing himself chairman of both the Fannie and Freddie boards. He later ousted the agency's acting inspector general and drove out hundreds of employees from the regulator and the government-backed mortgage businesses.

FHFA also pulled most of the watchdog’s funding a month ago, and OIG employees have been told as much as 80% of staff, or about 80 people, would be cut, Reuters previously reported.

WATCHDOG TRIES TO STAVE OFF CUTS

James Hodge, the acting head of the OIG, told lawmakers earlier this month the watchdog office would no longer be able to do its job following FHFA's budget cuts. The FHFA has defended the cuts by saying the OIG's budget and headcount are outsized compared to those for other regulators.

Since Hodge’s warning, OIG leaders have been talking with lawmakers about ways to stave off the mass job cuts. But staff have received furlough notices and have been told to prepare for reductions, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

The latest report to Congress marks a shot across the bow from the acting leader at the OIG. The office, like other such watchdogs, prepares a semiannual report for Congress that typically details OIG independence.

This is the first time in at least a decade that the office has flagged an instance of FHFA interference to its independence, according to a Reuters review of the semiannual reports.

According to the report, the OIG’s general counsel tried to convince the FHFA to cooperate with its evaluations by showing documentation of its congressionally mandated responsibilities.

The OIG is "entitled to access 'all records,'" the report said.

In mid-August, the inspector general’s office appeared to reach an "understanding" with the agency as to its role, the report said. But two weeks later, FHFA notified its inspector general it was "drastically reducing" the office's funding, the report said.

"The unprecedented and abrupt cuts will prevent OIG from conducting meaningful oversight of FHFA going forward," the report said, calling them "an extreme escalation of the Agency’s challenge to the OIG’s authority and independence."

data.title: Seegnal terminates older non-brokered private placements, launches new offering
data.description:
Key points:
  • Seegnal () said on Friday that it will terminate its previously announced non-brokered private placement offerings after raising aggregate gross proceeds of C$416,220.
  • The offerings terminated were announced on June 2, 2026; July 21, 2026; August 26, 2026; and October 1, 2026.
  • Following a review of its financing requirements and strategic alternatives, the company determined not to proceed with any additional tranches of the offering, as it is evaluating alternative financing opportunities that it believes may be more suitable for its current objectives, Seegnal said.
  • The company also launched a new non-brokered private placement of up to 1M units for gross proceeds of up to C$1.5M, at a price of $0.15 per unit.
  • Each unit is comprised of one common share and one common share purchase warrant. 
  • Each warrant is exercisable to acquire one common share at a price of C$0.25 for a period of 36 months from the applicable closing date.
  • The company added that it will use the proceeds from the new offering for general corporate and working capital purposes. 
  • All securities issued under the new offering will be subject to a hold period expiring four months and one day from the date of issuance. 
  • The offering is expected to close in one or more tranches on or before December 31, 2026.

data.title: Fitch Lowers France's Outlook to Negative From Stable
data.description:
By Stephen Nakrosis

Fitch Ratings said it was lowering its outlook on France's credit rating to negative from Stable, while affirming the country's A+ ratings.

The move comes as France faces economic and social pressure over its debt and growing borrowing costs. In recent weeks, hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Paris and other French cities, with some protesters resorting to vandalism and violence.

Fitch said the negative outlook reflects a deterioration since its August review, and cited weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a wider deficit. These factors are worsening debt dynamics from an already weak starting point, Fitch added.

Yields on France's government bonds have also risen since the last review, Fitch said. The agency said it now forecasts interest payments will increase to 3.3% of GDP in 2028 from 2.5% of GDP in 2025. Fitch also sees France's deficit at 5.5% of GDP in 2027, which it said reflects a weaker growth assessment and the risk of concessions during the budget process.

The country's A+ rating is supported by a large, wealthy and diversified economy, strong institutions, euro area membership and a resilient banking sector, Fitch added.

The next scheduled review date for France's rating hasn't yet been set, Fitch said, but added it expects to review the rating by end-February 2027 at the latest.

data.title: S&P Global revises Meta's outlook to 'negative' on AI spending, cash flow concerns
data.description:
S&P Global Ratings on Friday revised its outlook on Meta Platforms to "negative" from "stable", citing significant uncertainty around its capital spending and free operating cash flow.

Meta has been pouring money into advanced chips and data centers to compete more aggressively with AI market leaders, eroding its historically strong free cash flow.

The company's ability to monetize its AI investments is more limited than that of its peers, S&P said, adding it was unclear when its revenue streams would generate material contributions exceeding their rising costs over the next few years.

Meta last week forecast annual capital expenditure between $135 billion and $145 billion after reporting a free cash flow deficit of $2.12 billion in the third quarter, compared with positive free cash flow a year earlier.

"Given the lack of clarity around the company's future capex and its very ambitious multi-year AI investment plans, we are less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated," S&P said.

The ratings agency said it believes Meta's leverage could rise to above 1.0x as early as 2027, which is S&P Global's threshold for the "AA-" issuer credit rating.

S&P now forecasts Meta will generate free operating cash flow deficits of $39 billion in 2026 and $71 billion in 2027, adding that elevated capital spending could result in its FOCF remaining negative beyond 2028.

The social media company recently said it plans to sell $97.5 billion in stock in an effort to tap public markets as it expands AI infrastructure.

Meta's shares were little changed in extended trading on Friday. They fell more than 4% this week, marking their fifth straight weekly loss.

data.title: Wendy's and IHOP Face Buyout Bids. Going Private Is Easy, Fixing a Business Is Hard. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Evie Liu

Private-equity firms are targeting struggling U.S. restaurant chains, betting they can acquire the beaten-down businesses, revive their fortunes away from public-market scrutiny, and eventually cash out.

But a successful turnaround is not guaranteed.

This time around, the takeover bids are coming as the restaurant industry faces mounting pressure: at the same time elevated food and labor costs are squeezing margins, budget-conscious consumers are cutting back on eating out.

The challenge is particularly difficult for mature national chains. They need to invest in store renovations, menu innovation, technology, and marketing to regain customers, but weaker sales could constrain their ability to spend when earnings are constantly under watch.

Private ownership could offer some breathing room. Without quarterly earnings expectations and daily stock-price scrutiny, companies can pursue multiyear turnarounds, close underperforming locations, and accept temporary profit declines.

That prospect has attracted investors looking to take struggling restaurant chains private.

On Wednesday, Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management and partners offered $7.35 a share in cash to acquire Wendy's, a 20% premium to Tuesday's closing price. Wendy's said an independent board committee is evaluating the unsolicited, nonbinding offer.

On the same day, Bloomberg reported that Dine Brands, owner of Applebee's and IHOP, received an acquisition offer of $39 a share from Cobblers Cove Capital and Arkhouse Management, citing people familiar with the matter.

Dine Brands hasn't confirmed the reported offer, but said on Thursday that it had adopted a shareholder rights plan — commonly called a poison pill — to prevent investors from gaining control without paying shareholders an appropriate premium.

In March, The Wall Street Journal reported that Papa John's had attracted interest from Qatari-backed Irth Capital. But Papa John's appears reluctant to sell, noting that executing its own turnaround plan offered the best opportunity to create value.

A few restaurant chains have already left public markets. Denny's completed its acquisition by TriArtisan Capital, Treville Capital, and Yadav Enterprises in January. Last year, sandwich chain Potbelly was acquired by RaceTrac, a privately held convenience-store operator.

It's not uncommon for restaurant companies to move between public and private ownership as market conditions shift.

Following the financial crisis, Burger King went private in a $4 billion acquisition by 3G Capital in 2010. The burger chain returned to public markets less than two years later, allowing 3G to cash out part of its investment with gains.

Likewise, Bloomin' Brands, parent of Outback Steakhouse, returned to the stock market in 2012, five years after being taken private by Bain Capital and other investors. Dave & Buster's and Krispy Kreme have followed a similar path as well.

But private ownership isn't a guaranteed solution. Buyout firms often rely heavily on borrowed money to finance acquisitions, potentially saddling already-struggling restaurant chains with additional debt. Cost-cutting might also undermine food quality, service, and franchisee relationships.

Apollo Global Management took Carl's Jr. and Hardee's parent CKE Restaurants private in 2010. But CKE's attempted return to public markets in 2012 faltered amid concerns about its heavy debt load. California Pizza Kitchen, taken private by Golden Gate Capital in 2011, filed for bankruptcy nine years later, burdened by debt and pandemic-related disruptions.

Inspire Brands, the Roark Capital-backed owner of Dunkin', Arby's and Buffalo Wild Wings, filed confidentially for an initial public offering in May, hoping to raise capital to pay down debt. But The Wall Street Journal reported in September that the company was unlikely to go public this year unless restaurant stocks recovered.

To be sure, not every buyout involves additional borrowing. Trian's latest Wendy's proposal, for example, explicitly says the transaction wouldn't require new debt.

For shareholders, a takeover premium offers a potential exit from years of disappointing returns, but it doesn't guarantee a successful turnaround. Changing ownership is easy, changing the business is harder.

data.title: Binance Hit By Record $6.3 Bln Crypto Hack
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, suffered a $6.3 billion security breach in what analysts described as potentially the largest financial theft ever recorded.

The exchange halted withdrawals after hackers compromised its transaction approval system and transferred assets from an internet-connected wallet. Binance said customer funds remain safe and it has set aside about $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the losses. Around $3 billion of the affected assets have so far been located or frozen.

Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis said the attack showed similarities to previous cryptocurrency thefts attributed to North Korea. Binance is working with U.S. authorities, including the FBI and Secret Service, as investigators trace the stolen funds.

Tether froze nearly $1.57 billion linked to the breach, while Circle froze more than $800 million. The attack also pressured cryptocurrency markets, with bitcoin falling to a six-week low of $76,368 and ether dropping more than 3 percent to a two-month low of $2,178.
